sections.html:
Every Kansas eviction opens with a written notice from the landlord. Only after the notice runs out can the landlord ask a judge for possession. Neither the notice nor the courthouse can be skipped.

The reason for the eviction sets the notice. For unpaid rent, K.S.A. 58-2564 lets the landlord terminate the rental agreement if the tenant hasn't paid within three days of written notice, counted as three consecutive 24-hour periods. Mailing adds two days. The notice can be handed to the tenant, handed to someone over 12 years old who lives there, or posted in a conspicuous place on the premises.

A lease breach unrelated to rent gets a notice describing the problem. The tenant has 14 days to fix it, and if the problem remains, the agreement ends no sooner than 30 days after the notice is received. A similar breach later on can bring a 30-day termination notice with no second chance to cure.

One practical point: a separate three-day notice to leave must also precede filing, although a single document can do double duty as the termination notice and the notice to leave.

A typical Kansas eviction case can take up to 42 days from petition to writ. The landlord files in the district court of the county where the house sits.

StepWhat happensTiming
PetitionLandlord files; may add a claim for unpaid rentHearing set 3 to 14 days after filing
SummonsTenant is served and must answer in writing or appearOn or before the hearing date
Bench trialJudge hears both sides if the tenant contestsWithin 14 days of the hearing date
JudgmentJudge rules on possessionAt or after trial
Writ of restitutionSheriff or process server removes the tenantExecuted within 14 days

The governing statutes are K.S.A. 61-3801 through 61-3808, and the Kansas Judicial Branch self-help page walks through the process. A tenant who misses the first date risks a default judgment, which gives the landlord everything the petition asked for.

A tenant who loses may be ordered out quickly, in some cases within 24 hours. For anyone planning a sale around a vacant house, the writ date is the deadline that counts.

sections.h2: What a landlord can never do
sections.html:
Changing the locks, cutting off utilities or otherwise forcing a tenant out without a court order is off limits. K.S.A. 58-2569 bars a landlord from taking possession by action or by interrupting electric, gas, water or other essential service, with exceptions for abandonment or surrender.

Forcible removal belongs to the people authorized to carry out a writ of restitution. A tenant who is locked out or shut off may be able to sue in small claims court for up to one and one-half months of rent, or for damages if that is greater, potentially including punitive damages.

Owners selling a rented house sometimes feel pressure to speed things up. Shortcuts can create a claim against the owner that outlives the sale.

Kansas sets a defined path for abandoned belongings:

  • The landlord can store the property at the tenant's cost, sell it or dispose of it, but not until 30 days after taking possession.
  • Notice must be published in a newspaper in the county, giving the tenant's name, a description of the items and the disposal date.
  • A copy of the notice is mailed to the tenant's last known address.
  • The tenant can claim the items within the 30 days by paying storage, publication and similar costs.

Sale proceeds go first to storage costs and then to other debts the tenant owes. When a house has to be emptied before closing, this step most often delays the handoff to a buyer.

sections.h2: County programs that help avoid trial
sections.html:
Three of the largest counties run programs through their district courts.

  • Douglas County: an Eviction Resolution Program with a coordinator who connects both sides to rental assistance, legal aid and mediation.
  • Johnson County: an Eviction Mediation Program where a neutral mediator helps the parties reach an agreement before trial.
  • Sedgwick County: an Eviction Resolution Program that explains the court process and points to financial help, legal aid, mediation and emergency housing.

A landlord who plans to sell can use these programs to settle on a move-out date by agreement. A signed agreement with a firm date is often easier on a buyer than a contested case.

Former tenants have one more option. Some Kansas eviction cases can now be expunged, removing the court record from public view (2026 Substitute for House Bill 2357), and the courts run an online portal for people who file without a lawyer.

sections.h2: When the occupant is not a tenant
sections.html:
The residential landlord and tenant act doesn't cover someone who enters and stays with no rental agreement and without the landlord's knowledge, knowing they have no right to be there, after the landlord has personally told them to leave. Under K.S.A. 58-2573 such a person may be prosecuted for criminal trespass.

Where no landlord-tenant relationship exists and no other notice period applies, notice must be delivered at least three days before the petition is filed. Criminal trespass is a class B nonperson misdemeanor, with up to six months in county jail, a fine up to $1,000, or both. Only a county or district attorney, or a city prosecutor under a city ordinance, can bring those charges.

Kansas adverse possession takes 15 years of open, exclusive and continuous possession under K.S.A. 60-503, so an unwanted occupant of a few months has no ownership claim. The owner still has to use the eviction process or the trespass route rather than self-help.

sections.h2: Selling a rented Kansas house during an eviction
sections.html:
Selling a rented house doesn't end the tenant's rights, and an eviction in progress doesn't stop a sale. Under K.S.A. 58-2554, a landlord who sells in a good-faith sale to a bona fide purchaser is relieved of liability under the rental agreement for events after written notice of the sale goes to the tenant. The seller stays liable for any part of the security deposit the tenant is owed.

The deposit catches owners off guard. If you sell with the tenant in place, it doesn't vanish at closing, so the closing paperwork should say who holds it and who answers to the tenant.

Owners in this spot usually weigh three paths:

  • Finish the eviction first and hand over a vacant house, accepting the notice and court timeline above.
  • Sell with the tenant in place and give the written notice the statute describes.
  • Negotiate a move-out with the tenant, using a county mediation program if one exists.

Cash Home Buyers buys houses as-is, including some with tenants or damage left behind. Tell us what stage the case is in and we can talk through which path fits. A Kansas attorney should confirm the legal steps for your file.

The Kansas Judicial Council publishes eviction forms with instruction sheets for landlords and for tenants who respond. The nonpayment instructions tell the landlord to complete a civil cover sheet, mark the landlord and tenant forcible detainer category, and submit an eviction summons to the clerk. Service can be by sheriff, process server or return receipt delivery, and the clerk quotes the filing fee unless the filer submits an affidavit of inability to pay.

Kansas Legal Services runs an intake line at 316-267-3975. The self-help page also lists the Kansas Housing Resource Corporation, 211 Kansas and HUD resources for people who need rental help.

faqs.q: How long does a landlord have to wait after a three-day notice in Kansas?
faqs.a: Three days, counted as three consecutive 24-hour periods under K.S.A. 58-2564, plus two more if the notice is mailed. The landlord can then file a petition in district court.

faqs.q: How long does a Kansas eviction take once it is filed?
faqs.a: Up to 42 days is typical. The hearing is set within 3 to 14 days of filing, a trial within 14 days of that hearing, and the writ is executed within 14 days.

faqs.q: Can a Kansas landlord evict by shutting off the water or changing the locks?
faqs.a: No. K.S.A. 58-2569 prohibits it, and a tenant may be able to sue for up to one and one-half months of rent or damages.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Kansas rental while an eviction is pending?
faqs.a: Yes, nothing in the statutes bars it. Under K.S.A. 58-2554 the seller is relieved of later liability only after written notice of the sale goes to the tenant, and still owes any deposit the tenant is entitled to.

faqs.q: Can a Kansas eviction record be removed?
faqs.a: Some eviction cases can now be expunged under 2026 Substitute for House Bill 2357. The courts provide an online portal for people who represent themselves.
